slides.title: Solving Systems by Graphing
slides.note: Post the learning target. Today is 43 minutes: the cut is under Materials in the Lesson Plan.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is Notes I's table: three x's, three y's, three points. Say that after the reveal. Two minutes silent, then reveal, no discussion — 43 minutes today: the cut is under Materials.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Four phrases, read once each. The table is the tool all period: x = 0 first, then two more, and the third point is the check. 'Solve by graphing' ends with a check in both equations, every time. The coefficient of x is Monday's 'number multiplying x' with its proper name (Unit 10 gives it a second one); it decides parallel — 2 and −2 are equally steep but not the same direction, so they cross.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the table and the line.
slides.note:
The class has never drawn y = mx + b, so the line comes from a table. x = 0 first, then two more; put each x in and get its y. Plot the three points. Two points draw a line; the third is the check — three points in a row, or a y is wrong. Then draw the line through them and PAST them, to the edge of the grid: the crossing may be beyond the points you plotted.
OFF: 'Pick three x's. Find each y. Three points in a row, then a ruler through them, edge to edge.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
A table for each equation, both lines on one grid. They cross at (2, 3), and that is the solution — the one point on both lines. Then the check, every time: 2 + 1 = 3 and −2(2) + 7 = 3. Point out that the tables already agree at x = 2 (both give 3): the crossing shows in the tables too.
OFF: 'Graph both. Read the crossing. Check it in both equations.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Monday's pictures (11.05 Notes III), now with their reasons from the equations; no picture here. Parallel: y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x − 2 — the coefficient of x is 2 in both, so the lines climb at the same steepness in the same direction and stay 5 apart — parallel, no solution. Two level lines, y = 4 and y = −1, are parallel too: 0 multiplies x in both. One line: y = 3x − 1 and y = −1 + 3x make the same table (−1, 2, 5), so their graphs are one line: infinitely many solutions — and y = ½x + 1 and y = 0.5x + 1 are one line too, because ½ and 0.5 are one number. Then the bridge, line by line, said and not practiced: where Notes II's lines cross, both give the same y, so x + 1 = −2x + 7 — 11.02's equation; add 2x to both sides, take 1 from both sides, divide by 3: x = 2. It is how a graphed answer is checked; nobody is asked to do it today.
OFF: 'Same coefficient of x, different numbers added: parallel. One equation written two ways: one line.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: This is the model, and its question slide is empty on purpose: two tables with no y's and a grid with no lines. Work it on the projected slide in this order, saying each move: fill the first table (x = 0 first); plot its three points; rule the line through them and past them, edge to edge; the second table, its points, its line; then the crossing; then the check in both. Ask the room where the lines cross before anyone says it.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: The tables: 2x − 3 gives −3, −1, 1 and −x + 6 gives 6, 5, 4 at x = 0, 1, 2. The lines cross beyond the tables, at (3, 3) — which is why each line is drawn past its points. Check in both: 2(3) − 3 = 3 and −3 + 6 = 3. A board with (3, 0) or (0, 3) read a line where it meets an axis.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Two parts, five minutes. (1) Boards, two minutes: the tables at x = 0, 1, 2 give −2, −1, 0 and 6, 3, 0 — both give 0 at x = 2, so the lines cross at (2, 0), on the x-axis. A board with (0, 2) swapped the coordinates; with 'no solution', saw a crossing on an axis and did not count it. (2) Hand out the Independent Set now: everyone draws question 1 on its grid, three minutes, while you circulate — the first lines this class draws are drawn where you can see them. Look for a third point off the line (a y is wrong) and a line stopped at its last point (it can miss the crossing).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: A ½ multiplying x: choose even x.
slides.note: Ask what x's make ½x easy before anyone fills a table: the even ones, so x = 0, 2, 4. Then fill, plot and draw on the projected empty grid, as in Example 1.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Even x for the ½: at x = 0, 2, 4, ½x + 1 gives 1, 2, 3 and −x + 4 gives 4, 2, 0. Both tables give 2 at x = 2, so the lines cross at (2, 2). Check: ½(2) + 1 = 2 and −2 + 4 = 2. An odd x works too (x = 1 gives 1.5) — it is only harder to plot.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Even x again: at x = 0, 2, 4, ½x + 3 gives 3, 4, 5 and −x + 9 gives 9, 7, 5. Both give 5 at x = 4: the lines cross at (4, 5). Check: ½(4) + 3 = 5 and −4 + 9 = 5. A board with (5, 4) swapped the coordinates; one with (2, 4) or (2, 7) read one table only.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Read the crossing on the grid lines: x = 2, y = 4. Check it in both: 2 + 2 = 4 and −2 + 6 = 4. A board with (4, 2) swapped the coordinates; one with (0, 6) or (0, 2) read where a line meets the y-axis.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: No graph needed: the solution is the column where both tables give the same y. At x = 3 both give 4, so (3, 4). A board with (4, 3) swapped it; one with (4, 4) wrote the shared y for x as well; one with (2, 1) took the column x = 2, where the two y's (1 and 3) are closest before they meet — near is not equal. Check (3, 4) in both aloud.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: The crossing sits on the x-axis, at x = −2: (−2, 0). Check: 2(−2) + 4 = 0 and 2 − 2 = 0. A board with (0, −2) swapped the coordinates — (0, −2) is where the second line meets the y-axis, so it is a doubly tempting slip.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic: the four points a graph offers — the crossing (2, 1), the crossing swapped, and two places where a line meets an axis. Read the crossing on the grid lines, then check it in both: −2(2) + 5 = 1 and 2 − 1 = 1. A vote for (1, 2) swapped it; one for (1, 0) or (0, 5) read a point that lies on one line only — check it in the other equation aloud. On a split: sixty seconds, convince your neighbor, re-vote.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: The pattern breaks: no crossing to read. The same number, 2, multiplies x in both, so the lines climb at the same steepness and the first is always 5 above the second. A board with a point read a spot where the lines look close; one with 'infinitely many' saw two lines that go on forever.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic, and today's second IXL skill (write a system from a graph): read the four marked points — (0, 1) and (1, 3) on one line, (0, 4) and (2, 2) on the other; (1, 3) is on both lines, the crossing. Each equation must pass through both points of its line. Option C fits (1, 3), where the lines cross, and not (0, 1); option D makes the falling line rise; option B swaps the multiplier and the added number in both. The TE may say slope and y-intercept for B; the room says 'the number multiplying x'.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the \$3 is not needed. The crossing is (4, 4): x = 4 hours and y = 4 cm, so after 4 hours both candles are 4 cm tall. Check: −2(4) + 12 = 4 and −4 + 8 = 4. A board with 'after 3 hours' used the price.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Backwards: the point is given and a number of the second equation is missing. Put x = 2 and y = 5 into it: 5 = −2 + □, so the box is 7. Check the first too: 2(2) + 1 = 5. A board with 3 took 5 − 2 instead of 5 + 2.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence: the claim that two lines must meet somewhere. Read two aloud. The TE may say 'the same slope'; the room says 'the same number multiplying x'.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.

slides.title: IXL
slides.note: IXL: every listed skill is required, SmartScore 67. Due by the Unit 11 test.
